summary: Records how the committees that select, confirm, and recall members of the IAB and IESG operate, collecting lessons that had been passed on only orally. It was replaced by RFC 2282.

eli5.summary: It is a handbook for the people who pick the leaders. Past picking committees wrote down their tips so new ones do not start from zero.

questions: how are iab and iesg members selected
what is the ietf nominating committee
how does the ietf pick iesg members
can you remove an ietf leader
subtitle: How the IETF community selects and recalls its leaders

tldr.problem: The Internet standards process depends on the IAB (Internet Architecture Board) and IESG (Internet Engineering Steering Group), but the procedures for selecting, confirming, and removing these leaders had never been formally documented—only passed along by word of mouth.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2027 documents the nominating committee process: a committee of volunteers is randomly selected from the IETF community each year to nominate candidates for half the open seats, which are then confirmed by either the IAB or the Internet Society Board of Trustees. A separate recall process allows the community to request the removal of a leader for cause.
tldr.outcome: The process becomes transparent and consistent across multiple years, ensuring fair leadership selection and accountability. RFC 2027 was replaced by RFC 2282 to clarify and refine the procedures further.

today: RFC 2027 is a Best Current Practice document that was superseded by RFC 2282 in October 1996. RFC 2282 refined and clarified the procedures, particularly around mid-term vacancies and the timing of the process. The nominating committee process continues to be used annually by the IETF to select leaders, making it one of the longest-running mechanisms for open, community-based leadership selection.

sections.title: Why Document the Process
sections.content: The IAB and IESG are the bodies that oversee the Internet standards process. For years, the procedure for selecting, confirming, and recalling members had been executed multiple times (1992, 1993, 1994, 1995) but was documented only as an "oral tradition"—knowledge passed between successive nominating committees through informal discussions and email archives. This approach worked but created inefficiency and inconsistency. RFC 2027 formalizes the process that the community had evolved, making it transparent and repeatable. The document compiles lessons learned from four years of practice into a clear, written rulebook so future committees do not have to reinvent procedures or guess at best practices.
sections.eli5: Nobody wrote down the rules, so every year someone had to remember what the previous year's people did and explain it to the new volunteers. This RFC writes it all down so everyone knows what to do.

sections.title: Fundamental Rules
sections.content: Six key rules govern the entire selection and confirmation process. First, the nominating committee's job is to recruit and nominate candidates; it does not select which positions to fill—it is instructed what to fill. Second, the entire annual process (from selecting the committee to confirming all candidates) must complete within three months, with a specific timeline relative to the spring IETF meeting. Third, approximately half of the IESG and IAB positions are refilled each year, ensuring continuity and preventing massive turnover. Fourth, confirmed members serve at least a two-year term. Fifth, mid-term vacancies (due to resignation or recall) are filled by reconvening the most recent nominating committee with a compressed one-month timeline. Sixth, all deliberations are strictly confidential—committee members are exposed to sensitive information and must maintain secrecy. These rules ensure stability, fairness, and privacy.
sections.eli5: The committee just picks people for open jobs someone else tells them about. The whole thing takes 3 months. Only half the leaders are picked each year so the team is stable. People stay for 2 years. If someone quits early, there is a quick process to replace them. Everything is secret so people are honest.

sections.title: Selecting the Nominating Committee
sections.content: The nominating committee itself is selected through a transparent process. The committee consists of a non-voting Chair (appointed by the Internet Society President), at least 10 randomly selected voting volunteers from the IETF community, and two non-voting liaisons (one each from the IAB and IESG). To volunteer, a person must have attended at least 2 of the last 3 IETF meetings. Members of the Internet Society Board, sitting IAB members, and sitting IESG members cannot volunteer, to avoid conflicts of interest. The Chair publishes a call for volunteers, listing the open positions to help the community decide whether to volunteer for a position or the nominating committee. After the volunteers are identified, the Chair randomly selects 10 of them to be voting members. This random selection prevents bias and ensures the committee represents the broader community rather than being packed with allies of any particular person or position.
sections.eli5: A Chair (picked by the Internet Society President) finds volunteers from the community who have been to at least 2 of the last 3 meetings. The Chair then randomly picks 10 of those volunteers to be the voting committee members. This way nobody can stack the committee with their friends.

sections.title: How the Committee Does Its Work
sections.content: The nominating committee operates under a set of detailed rules. The Chair announces a call for nominations from the community; anyone can nominate any IETF member (including self-nomination) for any open position. The committee members deliberate together to select candidates they believe best fit the qualifications. Committee members cannot themselves be nominees—this prevents the selection process from becoming self-serving. Rejected nominees from the previous two years cannot be re-nominated, giving feedback time. Before announcing candidates, the committee advises the appropriate confirming body (the sitting IAB for IESG candidates, the Internet Society Board for IAB candidates). The confirming bodies then decide whether to confirm each candidate. If a confirming body rejects any candidates, the nominating committee reconvenes to select alternates. Strict confidentiality rules apply: candidate identities are secret until confirmed, nominee identities are secret (except the nominee may publicize their own intent), and rejected nominees and candidates are notified before any confirmations are announced. These rules preserve privacy while ensuring fairness.
sections.eli5: The committee calls for names, discusses candidates, and picks people they think are good. The committee members cannot be picked themselves. They tell the IAB and Internet Society people who they picked. If those people say no, the committee picks someone else. Everything stays secret until the confirmed people are announced.

sections.title: The Recall Process
sections.content: RFC 2027 includes a process for the community to remove a sitting IAB or IESG member if that person is not performing adequately. Anyone can request a recall by writing to the Internet Society President with justification. The President appoints a Recall Committee Chair who cannot be the person being recalled or the person requesting the recall. The recall committee is formed using the same rules as the nominating committee (with the same conflicts-of-interest exclusions). The committee investigates by giving the member a chance to present a written statement and by consulting with third parties. The committee votes on whether to recall the member. A 3/4 majority is required for a recall to succeed. If a member is recalled, the mid-term vacancy rules are applied to fill the position quickly. Though the RFC was written in 1996, the recall process had never been used up to that point, showing that the community has been satisfied with its leaders.
sections.eli5: If someone is doing a bad job, anyone can ask the Internet Society President to fire them. A new committee investigates, hears from both sides, and votes. It takes 3 out of 4 votes to fire someone. Then a new person is picked using the fast mid-term process.

sections.title: The Advice and Consent Model
sections.content: Throughout the process, an "advice and consent" model is used. The IETF Executive Director advises the nominating committee of open positions. The nominating committee advises the confirming bodies of candidates. The confirming bodies then consent (or refuse to consent). For IESG candidates, sitting IAB members review and decide whether to confirm. For IAB candidates, the Internet Society Board of Trustees reviews and decides. At least half of the confirming body members must agree on each decision. If all candidates are confirmed, the committee's work is done. If some are rejected, the committee must reconvene to find alternates. This model ensures that the nominating committee does the detailed recruiting work, but the responsibility for final approval rests with the appropriate body (leaders for IESG, the broader organization for IAB). This distributes power and prevents any single person or group from controlling the selection.
sections.eli5: It is not just one person picking leaders. The nominating committee suggests people, the IAB (for IESG jobs) or the Internet Society (for IAB jobs) has to agree, and at least half of them have to say yes to each person.
